paras: The Moscow, Tennessee, shooting and rescue of James Pettit was a January 1881 episode in which Charles Smith and James Pettit were accused of trying to outrage a fifteen-year-old girl at Moscow and shooting her brother, a Black stranger, as he defended her. Both men escaped custody, Pettit with the help of two masked men, and the papers disagreed on whether the brother died.
According to the Memphis Public Ledger, the man left Memphis with his sister on January 17 for "Saulsbury," Tennessee, but boarded the Somerville train by mistake and had to stop over at Moscow.

In the darkness, Smith and Pettit tried to outrage the girl, and when her brother tried to protect her, one held him while the other fired. The Ledger said he was shot; the Memphis Daily Appeal called it "the killing" of "a negro who was defending his sister."

Smith was arrested but got away the next day through his guards' carelessness. Pettit fled on a horse, which his pursuers shot from under him; he was retaken crossing Wolf River on a log and committed after a hearing. Two armed, masked men then freed him from his guard, a man named McCommon, in a Moscow store.

The Ledger reported that the community was "much stirred up" because the accused had sympathizers who kept the law from punishing them, and that the Somerville Reporter had called for a grand jury inquiry. No report of a recapture, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

Both Memphis papers carried the story on January 28, 1881, eleven days after the shooting. The Public Ledger headed its paragraph "Trouble at Moscow, Tennessee," called the attackers "ruffians" and "miscreants," and termed the affair a "disgraceful business." The Appeal, by contrast, gave one uncommented sentence among regional briefs.
On February 4 the Milan Exchange reprinted the Ledger's paragraph without credit, keeping its phrase "forty miles east of here."
The Ledger, the fuller account, said only that the brother was shot, while the Appeal said he was killed; no inquest or burial was reported.

reader.title: Moscow, Tennessee, shooting and rescue of James Pettit
bases: Two named men, not a mob, were accused of shooting a Black man who defended his sister from them, and two masked men later freed one of the accused from a guard (A2, A3); the violence against the Black victim was by individuals rather than a mob, posse or band.

The Public Ledger (A2) and the Memphis Daily Appeal (A3) agree on the attack, the two accused and the masked rescue, but the Ledger says the man was 'shot' while the Appeal calls it 'the killing'; the Milan Exchange (A4) only reprints the Ledger.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger report
accounts.gist: Smith and Pettit tried to outrage a Black stranger's sister in the dark and shot the brother, one holding him while the other fired; both escaped custody, Pettit finally with the help of two masked men, and the accused had local sympathizers.

accounts.label: Memphis Daily Appeal brief
accounts.gist: Pettit, accomplice of Charles Smith in the killing of a negro defending his sister on the seventeenth, was rescued by two armed and masked men from a guard in a Moscow store.

framing.detail: The Public Ledger headed it 'Trouble at Moscow, Tennessee', called Smith and Pettit 'ruffians' and 'miscreants' and the affair 'disgraceful business', and blamed sympathizers for thwarting the law.
The Memphis Daily Appeal ran a single sentence among regional briefs in 'News of Our Neighbors', without comment.

conflicts.note: The Ledger is the fuller account but says only 'shot'; the Appeal's brief calls it 'the killing'. Neither gives an inquest or burial, so the outcome is unresolved.

versions.value: shot by 'the ruffians', one holding him while the other fired

conflicts.note: The Ledger names Smith as the shooter in one sentence and attributes the shooting to both men in another; the Appeal calls Pettit Smith's accomplice.

info: The shooting occurred on or about January 17, 1881: the Appeal dates the killing to 'the seventeenth instant'; the Ledger says the victim left Memphis on the 17th and was forced to stop over at Moscow.
Moscow, Tennessee, 'forty miles east' of Memphis; Pettit was retaken at Wolf River and later rescued from a Moscow store.
An unnamed stranger described as 'a negro', travelling from Memphis toward 'Saulsbury', Tennessee, with his fifteen-year-old sister, who was the target of the attempted outrage.
No accusation was made against the victim; the two attackers, Charles Smith and James Pettit, were accused of attempting to outrage the girl and of shooting her brother.
Charles Smith and James Pettit (called 'ruffians'); for the later rescue, two unnamed masked men with pistols.
1 according to the Appeal ('the killing ... of a negro'); the Ledger says only that he was shot.
Two masked men freed Pettit from a guard named McCommon, and he had not been seen since; no recapture, indictment or trial of either man was found in the coverage.

sources.note: Full account 'Trouble at Moscow, Tennessee': Smith and Pettit attack a Black stranger's sister, shoot him; both escape custody; masked men free Pettit; cites Somerville Reporter.
quotes: The man Smith and another ruffian named James Pettit, undertook in the darkness to outrage the girl, whereupon the brother in trying to protect her, was shot by the ruffians
While in charge of a man named McCommon two masked men put pistols under his nose, and Pettit left, since which he has not been seen.
The community are much stirred up over the matter, as the miscreants have sympathizers who prevented the law from punishing them for their criminal work.
